Critics argue that the ads may oversimplify the environmental and social costs associated with large data‑center operations. Nonetheless, Build American AI maintains that its campaign will provide voters with a balanced view of the sector’s contributions to state economies. The group’s initiative underscores the growing influence of industry‑backed lobbying efforts in shaping public opinion on technology infrastructure policy.
author: TechCrunch

title: Polymarket raises $300 million from Donald Trump Jr.’s 1789 Capital fund
content:
1789 Capital, a venture‑capital firm known for backing technology and fintech enterprises, has taken the lead in a financing round that is projected to raise approximately $1 billion. The round, which includes participation from a consortium of institutional investors and strategic partners, is being positioned to provide the recipient company with substantial capital to accelerate product development, expand market presence, and pursue strategic acquisitions.

Industry observers note that the size of the round places it among the larger private‑equity transactions of the year, reflecting heightened investor confidence in the sector’s growth prospects. The infusion of funds is expected to support the company’s long‑term objectives while offering 1789 Capital a significant equity stake in the venture’s future performance.
author: TechCrunch

title: Apple claims former employee destroyed evidence of data theft
content:
Apple has confirmed that it possesses evidence indicating a former employee deliberately destroyed data that could have proven a data‑theft incident after learning he was under investigation. The company said the employee, who had previously worked in a role that involved handling sensitive information, deleted files and logs that were later recovered through forensic analysis. Apple’s statement notes that the evidence was obtained through internal audit procedures and that the employee’s actions violated the company’s data‑security policies.

According to Apple, the investigation was initiated after an anomaly was detected in the company’s data‑management system, prompting a review of access logs and user activity. The employee in question was notified of the investigation and subsequently took steps to remove or alter records that could have linked him to the breach. Apple’s legal team is currently assessing the extent of the damage and the potential regulatory implications, while the company has reiterated its commitment to maintaining robust data‑security protocols.

Apple’s spokesperson said the company will cooperate fully with any regulatory inquiries and that it is reviewing its internal controls to prevent similar incidents. The company has not disclosed the identity of the employee or the specific data involved, citing privacy and legal considerations. The incident underscores the importance of audit trails and the challenges organizations face in safeguarding digital evidence.
author: TechCrunch

title: Lachy Groom backs Indian startup aiming to keep aircraft aloft for a year
content:
Alteon, a startup founded by a 20‑year‑old entrepreneur, is engineering an autonomous aircraft designed to remain aloft for extended periods by harvesting wind energy. The company’s approach involves integrating lightweight turbine or sail‑based systems that convert ambient airflow into electrical power, enabling the aircraft to sustain flight for several months without conventional fuel.

The technology aims to address the growing demand for long‑duration, unmanned aerial platforms capable of persistent surveillance, communications, and environmental monitoring. By relying on renewable wind power, Alteon’s aircraft could reduce operational costs and carbon emissions compared with traditional battery‑ or fuel‑dependent drones. The firm is currently in the prototype testing phase, with plans to conduct longer‑duration flights later this year to validate the system’s endurance and reliability.
author: TechCrunch

title: Amazon sued by FTC and states over alleged ad pricing manipulation
content:
Amazon has replied to a lawsuit filed by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), asserting that the agency’s claims about the company’s advertising business are based on a misunderstanding of the market. In a statement, Amazon argued that its ad platform operates within the bounds of current antitrust law and that the FTC’s allegations fail to account for the competitive dynamics and consumer choice that characterize the digital advertising ecosystem.

The company’s response highlights its belief that the FTC’s investigation does not reflect the realities of how advertisers interact with Amazon’s services, and it maintains that its practices promote innovation and benefit consumers. Amazon has indicated it will continue to cooperate with regulators while challenging the FTC’s findings in court.
author: BBC Technology

title: Xi, Putin hold talks ahead of Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit
content:
Kyrgyzstan is hosting the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit, drawing the attendance of several heads of state, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. During the meeting, President Pezeshkian held bilateral talks with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, underscoring the event’s diplomatic significance.

The gathering marks the SCO’s 25th anniversary, a milestone the organization uses to highlight its expanding trade relationships among member nations. Over the past quarter‑century, the bloc has pursued deeper economic integration and positioned itself as a strategic counterweight to the United States‑led global order, promoting alternative frameworks for security and development.

As the summit concludes, officials emphasized continued cooperation and the intention to build on the anniversary’s momentum. The outcomes are expected to shape the SCO’s role in regional affairs and its broader influence on international economic and political dynamics.
author: France 24

title: Glacial flood in Nepal follows ice shelf collapse near Chinese border
content:
A sudden collapse of an ice shelf last Wednesday triggered a catastrophic flood that surged down more than 3,000 metres from the Chinese border into Nepal, according to reports from local authorities. The flood, which inundated several villages and damaged critical infrastructure, has raised immediate concerns about the region’s vulnerability to climate‑related hazards.

Scientists are now investigating whether the retreat of nearby glaciers, a trend linked to global warming, played a decisive role in the collapse. Preliminary data suggest that the rapid loss of ice mass may have weakened the structural integrity of the shelf, but researchers caution that additional factors—such as seismic activity and heavy rainfall—could also have contributed. Ongoing field studies and satellite monitoring aim to clarify the precise mechanisms behind the event.

The incident underscores the growing risk of glacial lake outburst floods in the Himalayas, a region already experiencing increased temperatures and glacial melt. As authorities assess the damage and plan for future mitigation, the international scientific community is urged to accelerate research into the links between climate change and glacial stability to prevent similar disasters.
author: France 24

title: EU suspends Brazilian meat imports over antibiotic compliance concerns
content:
The European Union announced on Thursday that it will suspend imports of Brazilian meat and other animal products, citing concerns that Brazil is not complying with EU regulations on antibiotic use in livestock. The ban covers poultry, beef, eggs and honey, and Brussels has made no commitment to a timeline for when trade can resume.  

The decision follows a series of inspections and investigations that revealed gaps in Brazil’s monitoring of antibiotic usage, which the EU says could undermine food safety and public health standards. Brazilian officials have expressed disappointment, arguing that the country has made significant progress in reducing antibiotic use and that the suspension could damage the livelihoods of millions of farmers and exporters.

The EU’s move is expected to impact trade flows and could prompt further diplomatic discussions between Brussels and Brasilia. Both sides will likely seek a resolution that satisfies EU safety requirements while protecting Brazil’s agricultural sector.
author: France 24

title: Arsenal Beat Aston Villa 1-0, Saka Scores
content:
Arsenal secured a 2‑0 victory at the Emirates Stadium, propelling the Gunners to six points in the Premier League and matching the tally of Manchester City, Hull City and Chelsea. The win came after a disciplined performance that saw Arsenal keep a clean sheet while capitalising on two early chances. The victory also kept the club firmly in the top four, maintaining a comfortable margin over rivals.

While Arsenal lifted the points, Aston Villa suffered a defeat that left them without a point, extending their winless run. Manchester City, Hull City and Chelsea also finished on three points each, each securing a win that helped them stay competitive in the league standings. Key moments included a decisive header from Arsenal’s striker in the first half and a late penalty that sealed the result.

With the win, Arsenal now sit comfortably in the top four, while Villa’s poor form has pushed them further down the table. The teams will look to build momentum ahead of their upcoming fixtures, with Arsenal aiming to maintain their position and Villa seeking a turnaround to avoid relegation pressure.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Poland launches terror investigation into drone factory fire
content:
Polish authorities have intensified their investigation into a series of sabotage incidents that appear to be linked to Russian intelligence, according to officials in Warsaw. The Ministry of the Interior and Administration confirmed that a comprehensive inquiry is underway, focusing on potential foreign espionage activities that may have facilitated the attacks on critical infrastructure. Investigators are examining evidence that suggests coordination with external intelligence agencies, with particular attention to the involvement of Russian operatives.

The inquiry follows a broader European security alert that has highlighted increased Russian interference in neighboring states. Warsaw has requested assistance from the European Union’s intelligence-sharing mechanisms and is coordinating with the United Kingdom’s intelligence services to trace the origins of the sabotage. Analysts say that the pattern of attacks—targeting energy facilities and transportation hubs—aligns with tactics previously attributed to Russian covert operations in the region.

While the full scope of the investigation remains confidential, Polish officials have reiterated their commitment to safeguarding national security. They emphasized that any confirmed links to foreign intelligence would prompt legal action and potential diplomatic repercussions. The government has urged the public to remain vigilant and to report suspicious activity to authorities as the probe continues.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Supreme Court Allows White House Ballroom Construction to Continue
content:
The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York issued a decision on Tuesday that replaces a temporary order issued earlier this month. The ruling concerns the ongoing litigation between pharmaceutical companies XYZ Pharmaceuticals and ABC Biotech over the use of a patented drug formulation.

The temporary order, issued on March 5, had barred ABC Biotech from marketing its version of the drug, citing infringement. In the new ruling, Judge Laura Martinez granted a permanent injunction that allows ABC to continue marketing under a licensing agreement, with specific royalty terms and quality‑control requirements. The court noted that the parties had reached a settlement agreement addressing the patent dispute and that the temporary order was no longer necessary.

The decision is expected to provide clarity for the market and reduce uncertainty for both companies. The parties will now comply with the new terms, and the case will be monitored for enforcement, underscoring the importance of resolving intellectual‑property disputes through negotiated agreements.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Journalists and Palestinians attacked in West Bank
content:
Violent attacks described by observers as pogroms erupted in the occupied West Bank, targeting Palestinian civilians and a crew from NBC News. The incidents unfolded on Saturday in the town of Qalqilya, where gunfire and stone‑throwing were reported near the main thoroughfare as the NBC team was filming a segment on settlement expansion. Several Palestinians were injured, and one NBC journalist sustained a minor concussion before the crew was escorted from the area by Israeli security forces.

Israeli police opened an investigation into the assaults, stating that they are reviewing footage and eyewitness accounts to identify the perpetrators. Palestinian officials condemned the attacks, accusing Israeli settlers of orchestrating the violence and demanding protection for both residents and journalists. International watchdog groups called for an independent inquiry, noting that similar confrontations have risen amid heightened tensions over settlement activity and restrictions on movement in the West Bank. The episode underscores the fragile security environment in the territory and the challenges faced by media personnel covering the conflict.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Three minors killed in Colombia armed group crackdown
content:
Rights groups have warned that armed groups are increasingly turning to social media to recruit children into their ranks. The organizations cite a rise in targeted messaging on platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp, and TikTok, where recruiters post propaganda, promises of money and status, and even livestream training sessions aimed at minors. The trend has prompted calls for stricter regulation of online content and tighter enforcement of existing child protection laws.

According to the reports, the recruitment strategy is part of a broader shift by non‑state armed actors to exploit digital channels that bypass traditional media scrutiny. Human rights monitors note that these groups often use encrypted messaging apps to coordinate with young recruits, offering them financial incentives or portraying participation as a means of gaining social recognition. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime has highlighted that such practices violate international conventions on the rights of the child and the prohibition of child soldiers.

The warning comes amid growing concerns that the digital age is making it easier for armed groups to reach vulnerable populations. While governments and civil society organizations are urged to strengthen online monitoring and provide counter‑narratives, the international community stresses the need for comprehensive measures to protect children from being drawn into armed conflict.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll resigns amid tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
content:
Washington – Deputy Secretary of Defense Michael Driscoll announced his resignation on Tuesday, ending a tenure that had been marked by escalating friction with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to multiple U.S. media outlets. The departure, effective immediately, follows several months of reported disagreements over budget allocations, procurement strategies, and the department’s approach to emerging security challenges.

Sources familiar with the internal dynamics said the tension began shortly after Hegseth assumed office, when the secretary pushed for a rapid overhaul of acquisition processes that Driscoll, a career defense official, viewed as premature. The two officials reportedly clashed in a series of closed‑door meetings, with Driscoll urging a more measured pace while Hegseth pressed for accelerated timelines. The discord spilled into public statements, as congressional staffers noted a growing divide between the department’s civilian leadership and its senior bureaucratic ranks. Driscoll’s resignation is expected to trigger a temporary reshuffling of senior staff as the Pentagon seeks to stabilize its leadership amid ongoing policy debates.

The exit underscores the challenges of aligning strategic vision within the Defense Department during a period of heightened geopolitical pressure. While the administration has not detailed a successor, officials indicated that an interim deputy will be appointed while a comprehensive review of the department’s leadership structure is conducted. The transition is likely to be closely watched by lawmakers and defense industry stakeholders as the Pentagon navigates its next phase of operational planning.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump says US will strike Iran after attacks on personnel in Jordan
content:
President Donald Trump announced that the United States will take action in response to recent Iranian strikes that targeted American personnel stationed in Jordan. The statement, delivered during a press briefing in Washington, came after reports confirmed that Iranian-backed militias had launched a series of rocket and drone attacks on a U.S. military base near the Jordanian capital, resulting in several injuries among service members.

The administration indicated that the forthcoming response will be “proportionate and decisive,” though specific measures were not disclosed. U.S. officials emphasized that the attacks violated international norms and threatened regional stability, underscoring a commitment to protect American forces abroad. The incident adds to escalating tensions between Tehran and Washington, with diplomatic channels remaining open as both sides assess the situation.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Tunisia's economy struggles and dissent shrinks five years after Saied's takeover
content:
Economic grievances continue to weigh heavily on Tunisians as the space for dissent narrows under President Kais Saied. Inflation remains above 10 percent, unemployment is hovering near 15 percent, and public debt has risen sharply, prompting frequent street protests and strikes across the country. The government’s response has been increasingly restrictive: authorities have detained dozens of activists, journalists and opposition figures, while new regulations tighten controls over social media and public assemblies. International observers note that the curtailment of civil liberties coincides with Saied’s broader consolidation of power since his 2019 election victory and the 2022 constitutional overhaul that expanded presidential authority.

The combined pressure of a faltering economy and limited avenues for political expression has heightened public frustration. While the administration argues that fiscal reforms and anti‑corruption measures are necessary to stabilize the nation’s finances, critics contend that the crackdown undermines democratic norms and hampers constructive dialogue. As Tunisia approaches the end of the current fiscal year, analysts warn that sustained economic hardship coupled with a shrinking civic space could fuel further unrest, prompting both domestic and foreign stakeholders to monitor the country’s trajectory closely.
author: Al Jazeera

title: DollyFest to serve as public memorial for Dolly Parton in Nashville and London
content:
Dolly Parton’s estate announced that a special edition of DollyFest will serve as the artist’s public memorial, fulfilling the country music icon’s expressed wish to celebrate her life with music rather than a conventional ceremony. The statement, released by the estate on Tuesday, confirmed that the festival will be held at Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, on the first weekend of November, marking the first time the annual event will incorporate a formal tribute component.

Organizers said the memorial-focused DollyFest will feature performances by a lineup of country and pop artists, a tribute segment highlighting Parton’s career milestones, and a charitable auction benefiting the Dollywood Foundation’s literacy and arts programs. Estate spokesperson Lisa McKinney emphasized that the format aligns with Parton’s long‑standing preference for “joyful celebration over solemn remembrance,” and that proceeds will continue to support the causes she championed throughout her career. The event is expected to draw tens of thousands of fans, providing a public homage that reflects Parton’s legacy of music, philanthropy, and community spirit.
author: BBC World

title: Man City agree £65m deal for Everton's Ndiaye
content:
Manchester City have confirmed the signing of Iliman Ndiaye from Everton, agreeing a deal worth a minimum of £60 million. The French midfielder, who has been a regular in the Premier League since joining Everton in 2020, will join City on a long‑term contract that will see him compete for a place in Pep Guardiola’s midfield rotation.

The transfer, completed in the summer transfer window, follows a period of speculation about the young talent’s future. City’s management cited Ndiaye’s technical ability and work rate as key factors in the decision, while Everton welcomed the financial boost that will help fund future squad reinforcements. The player is expected to undergo a medical and complete the necessary paperwork before joining the squad for pre‑season training.

With the deal in place, City’s midfield depth is set to increase ahead of the new season, while Everton will look to replace the departing midfielder with a combination of academy prospects and external signings. The move underscores both clubs’ strategic approaches to building competitive squads within the Premier League’s demanding environment.
author: BBC Sport

title: Messi's Decade of Dominance with Argentina Almost Didn't Happen
content:
Lionel Messi’s decade of dominance with Argentina will be remembered as one of football’s most remarkable narratives. Over ten years, the Argentine forward guided his national side from a period of uncertainty to a succession of triumphs, turning what many considered a near‑impossible dream into a reality that reshaped the country’s footballing identity.

During that span Messi collected a Copa América title in 2021 and a FIFA World Cup crown in 2022, becoming the first player to lift both trophies in a single decade. He also amassed 100 international goals, earned the Golden Ball at the World Cup, and consistently led the team in assists and match‑winning performances. His leadership on and off the pitch helped unify a squad that had previously struggled to find cohesion, and his individual brilliance—highlighted by record‑breaking goal tallies and decisive moments—cemented his status as a global icon.

The legacy of Messi’s decade-long run will endure in Argentine football lore and in the broader history of the sport. His achievements not only delivered silverware for a nation that had long yearned for success but also set new standards for consistency, resilience, and excellence on the international stage. As analysts and fans reflect on this era, Messi’s impact will be cited as a benchmark for future generations of footballers.
author: BBC Sport

title: Messi Announces Retirement from Argentina Duty
content:
Lionel Messi, the Argentine football legend, announced his retirement from international duty on Sunday, saying the decision was painful but inevitable. In a brief statement released through his social media channels, Messi acknowledged the emotional weight of stepping away from the national team, yet expressed confidence that the timing was right for him and the country.

Messi’s departure follows a career that has seen him win seven Ballon d'Or awards, lead Argentina to a Copa América triumph in 2021, and secure a historic FIFA World Cup title in 2022. The 36‑year‑old, who has been a central figure in Argentina’s midfield and attack for over two decades, confirmed that his focus will now shift to club football with Inter Miami, where he continues to contribute both on and off the pitch.

The Argentine federation and fans have praised Messi’s contributions, noting that his exit marks the end of an era for the national side. While the team will miss his leadership and skill, officials emphasized that the decision reflects Messi’s personal assessment of his future and the evolving needs of the squad.
author: BBC Sport

title: Trump Announces Medicaid Drug Pricing Deals with Nine Companies
content:
The Trump administration announced on Monday that it has struck new Medicaid drug‑pricing agreements with nine midsize biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies. In a statement released from the Oval Office, President Trump said the deals would ensure that “every drug will be at the lowest prices available anywhere in the world.” The agreements were signed in the presence of company executives and are intended to reduce the cost of prescription medications for state Medicaid programs.

Under the terms of the agreements, the companies will charge state Medicaid programs the same price that the federal government pays for each drug. The contracts cover a range of specialty medications, many of which are used to treat chronic and rare conditions. The administration claims the deals will provide predictable, low-cost access to essential therapies for millions of Medicaid beneficiaries across the country.

The agreements are part of a broader effort to curb rising prescription drug costs in the United States. While the administration has highlighted the potential savings for Medicaid recipients, critics have urged caution, noting that the long‑term impact on drug innovation and market competition remains unclear. The deals will be monitored by state Medicaid agencies to ensure compliance with the agreed pricing terms.
author: The Hill

title: House Democrats introduce bill to stop Trump renaming Lake Ontario
content:
A trio of House Democrats filed the “Hands Off Our Great Lakes Act” on Monday to prevent President Donald Trump from renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America,” a move he authorized last week with an executive order amid his ongoing trade dispute with Canada. The bill would bar the president and the Interior Department from issuing any further orders that alter the names of the Great Lakes, arguing that the renaming is an unnecessary political gesture that could undermine the lakes’ historic and environmental significance.

The legislation follows Trump’s broader strategy to assert U.S. dominance in trade negotiations, which has included tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum and a push to re‑brand Canadian assets as American. House Democrats contend that the executive order lacks congressional approval and that it sets a precedent for unilateral name changes that could affect other natural landmarks. The act also calls for a review of the executive order’s legal basis and seeks to restore the original names through congressional action.

The bill is now pending committee consideration, and its sponsors have urged lawmakers to act swiftly to preserve the integrity of the Great Lakes. If passed, the legislation would effectively reverse Trump’s renaming and reaffirm the lakes’ established names, while also limiting the president’s ability to alter geographic nomenclature without congressional oversight.
author: The Hill

title: Trump says it’s too early to discuss Hegseth 2028 run
content:
President Donald J. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday that it is premature to consider a presidential bid by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for the 2028 election. Trump emphasized that Hegseth is “doing a fantastic job” in his current role, suggesting that any future political ambitions should wait until the Secretary’s tenure is more fully evaluated. The president’s remarks came amid growing speculation among media outlets and political analysts about a potential Hegseth campaign.

In his brief statement, Trump acknowledged the chatter surrounding Hegseth’s possible candidacy but stressed that the administration’s focus remains on defense policy and national security matters. He added that the decision to run would depend on a range of factors, including the Secretary’s performance and the political climate at the time. The President’s comments were intended to reassure both the public and Hegseth’s supporters that the Secretary’s current duties remain the priority.

The Oval Office exchange underscores the administration’s intent to keep its focus on defense and foreign affairs while leaving open the possibility of future political developments. As the 2028 election cycle approaches, observers will watch closely to see whether Hegseth’s prospects evolve or if he continues to concentrate on his responsibilities as Defense Secretary.
author: The Hill

title: Judge permits forced feeding of Afghan accused of National Guard shooting
content:
U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta issued a brief ruling on Saturday allowing the Bureau of Prisons to force-feed Afghan national Rahmanullah Rahman, who is awaiting trial on charges that he ambushed two National Guard members during a patrol in Kabul last year. The judge’s order permits the BOP to provide “nonconsensual nutrition and medical treatment” to Rahman while he remains in custody, citing the federal prison system’s duty to maintain inmates’ health and safety.

Rahman was arrested in 2023 after a federal investigation linked him to a plot that resulted in the deaths of two U.S. soldiers. He is currently held at a federal facility pending trial. The judge’s decision follows a request from the Department of Justice, which argued that Rahman’s refusal to eat could jeopardize his health and impede the court’s ability to conduct a fair trial. The order does not address the underlying criminal case but establishes the prison’s authority to intervene in the inmate’s medical care.

The ruling underscores the balance courts must strike between respecting inmate autonomy and ensuring that prisoners receive necessary medical treatment. It also highlights the broader legal and humanitarian considerations that arise when inmates refuse food or medical care in federal custody. The case will proceed to trial, where the charges of ambush and conspiracy will be examined in detail.
author: The Hill

title: Trump approval dips to new low as Iran war weighs on support: Poll
content:
A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll released on Thursday found President Donald J. Trump’s job‑performance approval rating falling to a new low of 32 percent, the lowest level recorded in the university’s recent surveys. The national survey, which interviewed 1,000 respondents between August 21 and 26, shows a one‑point drop from the previous poll conducted earlier in the month.

The poll was carried out amid the prolonged conflict in Iran, a factor that many respondents cited as a key reason for their dissatisfaction. While the survey measured approval of the president’s performance rather than specific policy positions, the decline suggests a growing sense of discontent among the American public. The UMass Amherst poll is one of several university‑conducted surveys that track public opinion on national leadership.

The new figures underscore the challenges facing the administration as it navigates both domestic and international pressures. Though the poll does not predict immediate political action, the continued decline in approval may influence future electoral calculations and public discourse.
author: The Hill

title: Ivey Weighs Stopgap Bill as House Reopens
content:
NPR’s A Martinez interviewed Maryland’s Democratic Representative Glenn Ivey as the House of Representatives reconvened this week, with a temporary stopgap spending bill slated for discussion. The bill, designed to keep federal agencies funded through the end of the fiscal year, is a last‑minute measure intended to avoid a government shutdown while lawmakers negotiate a longer‑term budget plan.

Ivey, who has been a key advocate for bipartisan fiscal responsibility, emphasized the importance of maintaining essential services and protecting the interests of Maryland’s constituents. He noted that the stopgap measure would provide a brief window for further negotiations and highlighted the need for a comprehensive budget that addresses both immediate funding gaps and long‑term fiscal health. The bill’s passage is seen as a procedural step, but it also underscores the ongoing partisan divide over how best to manage federal spending.

The House’s decision to bring the stopgap bill to the floor reflects the urgency of preventing a shutdown, while also setting the stage for a more detailed budget debate. As lawmakers prepare to vote, the focus remains on balancing short‑term funding needs with the broader fiscal agenda that will shape the next phase of congressional deliberations.
author: NPR Politics

title: The U.S.-Venezuela oil deal won't lower your gas prices. Here's what you need to know
content:
The Trump administration announced on Friday a partnership to develop a large portion of Venezuela’s oil reserves, with the United States taking a majority stake in the venture. The agreement, signed with a Venezuelan state‑owned company, is intended to boost production in a country whose output has fallen sharply in recent years.

Industry analysts point to several concerns that could undermine the project’s viability. They cite Venezuela’s ongoing political instability, the deteriorating condition of its refineries and pipelines, and the lack of a clear legal framework for foreign investment. Additionally, the U.S. government’s own regulatory and environmental standards could complicate the development of the field.

While the deal signals a renewed U.S. interest in Venezuelan hydrocarbons, experts caution that the challenges outlined above may limit the project’s success. The administration will need to address these issues before the partnership can move beyond the initial announcement.
author: NPR Politics

title: Scholar discusses Trump's claims of a new Venezuelan oil agreement
content:
NPR host A. Martínez sat down with Francisco Monaldi, director of the Latin America Energy Program at Rice University, to examine President Donald Trump’s recent assertion that the United States had secured a new oil agreement with Venezuela. Monaldi clarified that no such deal has been announced by the Venezuelan government, and that the administration’s claims appear to be based on unverified information. He noted that any credible agreement would require transparent terms and a clear regulatory framework—none of which have been disclosed to the public.

Monaldi explained the broader context of U.S.–Venezuelan energy relations, highlighting the long‑standing sanctions that have effectively isolated Venezuela’s oil sector from international markets. He warned that the president’s statements could be a political maneuver to justify a hard‑line stance on the Venezuelan crisis, rather than a reflection of an actual contractual arrangement. The expert also pointed out that the U.S. oil industry’s current supply chain is already strained, and that a sudden influx of Venezuelan crude could destabilize prices and logistics.

In closing, Monaldi urged listeners to scrutinize the president’s claims and to await official confirmation before drawing conclusions. He emphasized that any future agreements would need to be vetted through rigorous diplomatic and economic channels to ensure they serve both U.S. and Venezuelan interests.
author: NPR Politics

title: Business groups urge scrapping of food price cap plan
content:
More than 20 organisations have jointly addressed John Swinney, requesting that he abandon a proposed legal cap on the prices of certain food and drink items. The letter, signed by a mix of consumer advocacy groups, industry associations and local community organisations, was sent to Swinney’s office in Edinburgh on Monday. It argues that the cap would distort market dynamics and could lead to unintended shortages or reduced supply of affected products.

The proposed cap, which would set maximum prices for a range of packaged foods and alcoholic beverages, was introduced as part of the Scottish Government’s cost‑of‑living package. Critics in the letter contend that the measure would disproportionately affect small retailers and producers, potentially driving up costs elsewhere in the supply chain. They also note that similar price‑control initiatives in other jurisdictions have led to reduced product availability and increased black‑market activity. The organisations call for a review of the policy and suggest alternative support measures that would target households more directly without interfering with market pricing.

Swinney has not yet issued a public response to the letter. The Scottish Government is expected to consider the feedback as it finalises the policy, with a potential review of the cap’s scope and implementation timeline. The debate highlights the broader challenge of balancing consumer protection with market freedom in the context of rising living costs.
author: BBC Politics

title: Conservatives warn early release could free dangerous criminals
content:
Prime Minister Alexei Petrov announced that a limited number of inmates serving indefinite sentences could be released to alleviate overcrowding in the country’s prisons. The proposal, aimed at increasing available capacity for new detainees, was met with an immediate warning from the National Prison Authority, which cautioned that the policy could undermine the integrity of the judicial system and compromise public safety.

The authority’s statement highlighted concerns that early releases might create a perception of leniency, potentially eroding public confidence in the criminal justice process. It also noted that the current legal framework does not provide clear guidelines for determining which prisoners would qualify for such releases, raising questions about fairness and consistency. The government has said it will review the proposal in consultation with legal experts and prison officials before any decisions are made.

In response, the Ministry of Justice pledged to conduct a comprehensive assessment of the policy’s impact on prison operations and community safety. Officials emphasized that any changes would be implemented only after thorough evaluation of risks and benefits, with the goal of maintaining the balance between rehabilitation and security.
author: BBC Politics

title: Stride and Patel Replaced in Tory Reshuffle Ahead of October Conference
content:
Conservative MP Kemi Badenoch announced a reshuffle of her senior advisory team on Thursday, ahead of the party’s October conference. The move comes as she prepares to play a more prominent role in the upcoming leadership contest and seeks to strengthen the support structure around her policy agenda. Badenoch said the changes would bring fresh perspectives to her office and improve coordination across her policy priorities.

Key appointments include the promotion of senior adviser James Patel to chief of staff, a role that will oversee day‑to‑day operations and strategic planning. In addition, former campaign manager Sarah O’Neill has been named deputy chief of staff, while the position of communications director has been filled by veteran political journalist Liam O’Connor. Badenoch also announced the creation of a new policy unit focused on digital infrastructure, headed by former ministerial aide Priya Desai. The reshuffle signals her intent to present a cohesive, modernised team at the conference, where she is expected to outline her vision for the party’s future.

Badenoch’s announcement was framed as a step toward consolidating her leadership credentials and ensuring a smooth transition of responsibilities. By tightening her inner circle, she aims to demonstrate organisational readiness and policy depth to party members and voters alike. The reshuffle will be closely watched as the party gears up for its October gathering, where leadership dynamics and policy priorities will be on the agenda.
author: BBC Politics

title: India Calls for Timely Climate Adaptation Finance Ahead of COP31
content:
India’s climate strategy is coming under scrutiny as the world prepares for the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP 31).  New reports highlight that the country is not only demanding higher levels of adaptation finance from the international community, but also insisting that the money be released promptly to support projects that can mitigate the impact of extreme weather events, such as the devastating floods that hit Assam last year.  The floods, which displaced hundreds of thousands and caused widespread damage, underscored the urgent need for timely investment in resilient infrastructure and early‑warning systems.

The Indian government has argued that adaptation spending must be treated as a long‑term investment rather than a short‑term relief measure.  It points to the lag between pledges and actual disbursement as a critical bottleneck, noting that delays can render even well‑designed projects ineffective.  In the lead‑up to COP 31, India is calling for clearer mechanisms and faster disbursement timelines from donor countries and multilateral institutions to ensure that adaptation projects reach the ground before the next wave of climate‑related disasters.

If the international community heeds India’s call, the country could strengthen its disaster‑risk reduction capacity and set a precedent for other developing nations facing similar climate pressures.  The outcome of COP 31 will likely determine whether adaptation finance is delivered as a timely investment that builds resilience or remains a delayed, piecemeal response to crises.
author: Climate Home News

title: Florida Man Urges Loved Ones to Hold Tight After Wife and Toddler Killed by Lightning
content:
A vigil held in a Florida community on Saturday honored the memory of Kenya Glasgow and her two‑year‑old daughter Kennedi, both of whom were killed by a lightning strike on August 23.  The tragedy, described by local authorities as an exceedingly rare event, left the family and neighbors stunned.  Kameron Glasgow, the husband, spoke to local media at the gathering, urging people to “hold … tight” to their loved ones in the wake of such sudden loss.

The ceremony took place at a quiet park near the family’s home, where mourners laid flowers and shared memories of Kenya’s warm personality and Kennedi’s bright spirit.  Glasgow, visibly moved, thanked the community for its support and highlighted the importance of community solidarity during grief.  He noted that the lightning strike, which struck the family’s backyard while he was nearby, was a freak occurrence that no one could have predicted.

Glasgow’s remarks underscore the need for emotional support and preparedness for unexpected disasters.  As the family continues to process the loss, the vigil served as a reminder of the fragility of life and the enduring strength of community ties in times of tragedy.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Grand Canyon Flash Flood Claims Two Lives, 15 Missing
content:
A second fatality has been confirmed in the Grand Canyon after a flash flood swept through the park over the weekend, the National Park Service (NPS) announced on Monday. The sudden surge of water and debris forced the evacuation of dozens of visitors by helicopter and destroyed sections of trails and park infrastructure. The NPS confirmed the death of a second individual, bringing the total number of fatalities from the event to two.

The agency reported that fifteen people remain missing or unaccounted for as additional heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast for the coming days. The NPS warned that these weather conditions could trigger further debris flows, flash floods, or rockfalls, potentially endangering more visitors and park personnel. Officials are continuing search and rescue efforts while monitoring the evolving storm threat.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Salmonella Contamination: Food, Pets, and Everyday Surfaces
content:
Salmonella, a bacterial pathogen that can cause severe gastrointestinal illness, has been identified in a wide range of environments, from grocery store produce and processed foods to household pets and public recreation areas. Health officials report that the bacteria can survive on surfaces and in soil, making it a common contaminant in both domestic and outdoor settings. Recent surveillance data indicate that the incidence of salmonellosis has remained steady, with outbreaks linked to contaminated eggs, poultry, fresh produce, and even pet food.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) notes that while most infections are mild, severe cases can lead to hospitalization, especially among young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. In response, food safety agencies have intensified inspections and enforcement of hygiene protocols in food production and handling facilities. Pet owners are advised to practice strict hand hygiene after handling animals and to keep pets’ food and water bowls clean to reduce the risk of cross‑contamination.

Public health guidance emphasizes routine handwashing, proper cooking temperatures, and safe food storage to mitigate exposure. Ongoing monitoring by federal and state authorities aims to track contamination sources and inform targeted interventions, ensuring that both foodborne and environmental Salmonella risks are addressed effectively.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Spatial transcriptomics maps may outperform biomarkers in predicting immunotherapy response
content:
Spatial transcriptomics has emerged as a cutting‑edge technique that simultaneously captures gene expression patterns and their precise spatial coordinates within a tissue section. By preserving the physical context of cells, the method generates high‑resolution maps that reveal how individual genes are activated across distinct cellular neighborhoods. This dual information—molecular activity and location—offers a comprehensive view of tissue architecture that was previously unattainable with conventional bulk or single‑cell sequencing.

The technology is particularly transformative for oncology, where the tumor microenvironment exerts a profound influence on cancer progression and treatment response. Spatial transcriptomics allows researchers to delineate the heterogeneity of tumor cells, immune infiltrates, stromal components, and vascular structures within the same sample. By correlating gene expression signatures with their exact positions, scientists can identify micro‑domains that drive drug resistance, metastasis, or immune evasion, thereby informing more precise therapeutic strategies.

As the field matures, spatial transcriptomics is expected to integrate with other modalities such as proteomics, imaging, and computational modeling, expanding its utility in both basic research and clinical diagnostics. The ability to map the dynamic interplay between genes and their microenvironment promises to accelerate the discovery of novel biomarkers and targeted interventions, ultimately improving patient outcomes.
author: Medical Xpress

title: AAN and AHS Release Updated Migraine Prevention Guideline for Adults
content:
The American Academy of Neurology (AAN) and the American Headache Society (AHS) have released a joint practice guideline update aimed at helping clinicians choose the most effective medications for preventing migraines in adults. The new recommendations, published in the journals *Neurology* and *Headache*, build on the 2012 guideline and incorporate the latest evidence from clinical trials and systematic reviews.

The update provides a detailed, evidence‑based ranking of preventive therapies, including beta‑blockers, antiepileptics, and newer monoclonal antibodies targeting calcitonin gene‑related peptide pathways. It also outlines patient‑specific considerations such as comorbid conditions, drug interactions, and tolerability profiles. The American Academy of Family Physicians has endorsed the guidelines, underscoring their relevance for primary care providers who often initiate migraine prevention.

By offering a clearer framework for medication selection, the revised guidelines aim to improve treatment outcomes and reduce the burden of migraine on patients and healthcare systems. Clinicians are encouraged to review the full recommendations to integrate them into routine practice.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Semen facilitates infection with mpox virus, study shows
content: Researchers at Goethe University and Universitätsmedizin Frankfurt have identified a mechanism by which seminal fluid facilitates the uptake of the mpox virus into host cells, offering new insights into the pathogen's evolving transmission dynamics. Historically, mpox was transmitted predominantly from animals to humans; however, recent outbreaks have been driven by new variants that exhibit an increased capacity for person-to-person
author: Medical Xpress

title: Estimated glucose disposal rate inversely linked to benign prostatic hyperplasia
content:
A recent study published online on August 25 in *The Aging Male* reports a negative association between estimated glucose disposal rate (eGDR) and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) in men. eGDR, a surrogate marker of insulin sensitivity, was calculated for a cohort of adult males and compared with clinical assessments of prostate enlargement. The researchers found that lower eGDR values, indicating poorer insulin sensitivity, correlated with higher prevalence and severity of BPH symptoms.

The investigators analyzed data from a cross‑sectional sample of men aged 50 to 75, controlling for age, body mass index, and comorbidities such as hypertension and dyslipidemia. After adjusting for these factors, each unit decrease in eGDR was associated with a statistically significant increase in the likelihood of clinically diagnosed BPH. The authors suggest that insulin resistance may contribute to prostatic growth through metabolic and inflammatory pathways, although causality cannot be established from this observational design.

These findings highlight a potential link between metabolic health and prostate disease, underscoring the importance of managing insulin sensitivity as part of comprehensive care for aging men. Further longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether improving eGDR can reduce BPH incidence or progression.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Higher vitamin B12 levels in both parents associated with a lower risk of birth defects
content:
A new prospective cohort study has identified protective associations between parental vitamin B12 levels before conception and maternal red blood cell (RBC) folate concentrations after conception with the risk of birth defects. Researchers measured these nutrients in a large sample of couples and followed the pregnancies to assess congenital anomalies. The analysis showed that higher preconception vitamin B12 in parents, as well as elevated maternal RBC folate during early pregnancy, correlated with a statistically significant reduction in birth defect incidence.

The investigators controlled for potential confounders such as maternal age, socioeconomic status, and smoking habits, strengthening the evidence that these micronutrients play a role in fetal development. The findings suggest that adequate vitamin B12 intake before conception and maintaining sufficient folate stores after conception may be important strategies for reducing the likelihood of congenital malformations. These results add to the growing body of literature supporting the benefits of balanced prenatal nutrition.

Public health agencies may consider these insights when designing preconception and prenatal care programs. Ensuring that prospective parents receive guidance on vitamin B12 supplementation and folate-rich diets could help lower birth defect rates, complementing existing folic acid recommendations aimed at preventing neural tube defects.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Manhattan's luxury rental market is booming, with units reaching $100,000 a month
content:
New York City real‑estate brokers report a sharp uptick in affluent renters, a trend that is pushing Manhattan rents to record highs. According to a recent survey of brokerage firms in the borough, the proportion of tenants willing to pay premium rents for luxury apartments has risen markedly over the past year.

The data show that the median rent for a one‑bedroom unit in Manhattan climbed to $4,800 in the third quarter, up 12 % from the same period last year, while two‑bedroom units reached $6,200, a 15 % increase. Brokers attribute the surge to a combination of low inventory, high demand from high‑net‑worth individuals, and the continued appeal of city living amid remote‑work flexibility. “We’re seeing more buyers transition to renters, especially those who can afford the premium for prime locations and top‑tier amenities,” said a spokesperson for a leading brokerage group.

If the current influx of wealthy renters persists, analysts warn that the upward trajectory could continue, tightening the market further and potentially prompting new zoning or housing‑policy responses. The trend underscores the growing divide between luxury and affordable housing in Manhattan and highlights the need for continued monitoring of rent dynamics across the city.
author: CNBC Business

title: Trump Secures Drug Pricing Deals with Nine Mid‑Sized Companies
content:
The United States has announced a series of new agreements that extend the Trump administration’s strategy of tying domestic drug prices to those in lower‑cost markets abroad.  The deals, signed this week with several European and Asian partners, formalize a framework that allows U.S. manufacturers to benchmark their pricing against the lowest rates paid in the partner countries.  By linking U.S. prices to these external benchmarks, the agreements aim to curb inflation in the pharmaceutical sector while maintaining market access for American drugs.

Under the new framework, U.S. drug companies will report pricing data from the partner markets and adjust their U.S. pricing accordingly, subject to oversight by the Department of Health and Human Services.  The initiative follows the Trump administration’s 2020 proposal to use international price comparisons as a tool for negotiating lower costs with insurers and pharmacy benefit managers.  The agreements also include provisions for data sharing, transparency, and periodic review to ensure that price adjustments reflect genuine cost differences rather than market manipulation.

These contracts are expected to accelerate the adoption of global price‑benchmarking practices in the United States, potentially reducing out‑of‑pocket expenses for patients and easing the financial burden on the healthcare system.  While critics warn that the approach could limit innovation incentives, supporters argue that the new deals provide a pragmatic pathway to more affordable prescription drugs without compromising access to life‑saving therapies.
author: CNBC Business

title: Mortgage rates hit highest level since June 2025 amid Middle East conflict
content:
The year’s monetary policy outlook shifted sharply after the outbreak of hostilities with Iran, a development that drove global oil prices higher and disrupted expectations of falling interest rates. Analysts had projected a gradual easing of rates to support economic recovery, but the sudden spike in energy costs has altered that trajectory.

The conflict has pushed Brent crude above $90 a barrel, a level not seen since 2014, and has tightened supply chains across the Middle East. Central banks, observing the inflationary pressure from elevated fuel prices, are now reassessing the timing and magnitude of rate cuts. The rise in oil prices has also amplified concerns about sustained inflation, prompting a more cautious stance from policymakers.

In light of these dynamics, market participants anticipate that the anticipated rate cuts may be delayed or scaled back. The interplay between geopolitical risk and commodity pricing continues to shape monetary policy decisions, underscoring the sensitivity of financial markets to global events.
author: CNBC Business

title: Starbucks Workers in Buffalo Unionize, Spark Corporate Pushback
content:
Mark Mori, a former Starbucks employee turned union organizer, praised the determination of workers in the Buffalo region of New York who began a public union‑organizing campaign in 2021 amid the COVID‑19 pandemic. The campaign, which started as a local effort to improve wages, benefits and working conditions, has grown into one of the largest union drives in the food‑service sector and has drawn intense scrutiny from Starbucks’ corporate leadership.

Starbucks has responded with a multi‑pronged strategy that includes legal challenges, public relations campaigns and the deployment of union‑busting consultants. The company’s actions have sparked a broader debate about labor rights in the hospitality industry, with the Buffalo workers citing unsafe working conditions and inadequate pandemic protections as key motivators for their push for collective bargaining. The union’s outreach has reached thousands of employees across the region, and the campaign has attracted national attention from labor advocates and policymakers.

The dispute remains unresolved, but the Buffalo campaign has highlighted the growing tension between large corporate chains and frontline workers seeking representation. As the legal and political battles continue, the outcome could set a precedent for future unionization efforts in the United States.
author: Guardian Business

title: Greer, Lutnick, Navarro lead US trade team amid Canada dispute
content:
US trade representative Jamieson Greer, known for his calm demeanor, found himself at the center of a diplomatic crisis after the collapse of trade talks with Canada. Despite his background—having read Victor Hugo’s *Les Misérables* in French while on a military tour in Iraq—Greer was unexpectedly accused of francophobia, a charge that has cast a shadow over his tenure. The dispute, which began over tariff disagreements on agricultural products and steel, now threatens to spiral into a full‑blown trade war between the two closely linked economies.

The situation has drawn attention from other key figures in the administration. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been tasked with negotiating a resolution, while White House adviser Peter Navarro has publicly criticized the talks’ breakdown, urging a more confrontational stance. Together, the trio faces the challenge of restoring stability to a partnership that underpins a significant portion of both nations’ trade volumes, while managing domestic pressures for a swift and decisive outcome.

If the negotiations fail to produce a mutually acceptable agreement, the United States and Canada could see a sharp rise in tariffs that would disrupt supply chains and increase costs for consumers. The administration’s next steps will be closely watched, as any escalation could have broader implications for North American trade dynamics and global markets.
author: Guardian Business

title: Kushner Regrets Joining FIFA World Cup Sell-Off Plan
content:
Venture capitalist Joshua Kushner has said he would not have taken part in former FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s abandoned proposal to sell stakes in the World Cup if he had known how the football community would react. The plan, which was revealed in early 2024, aimed to raise capital for the governing body by offering shares in the tournament’s revenue streams to private investors. It was met with swift criticism from clubs, players and fans, who argued that the World Cup’s legacy and integrity could be compromised by commercial interests.

Infantino’s proposal was ultimately shelved after a backlash that included protests from major football associations and a formal objection from the International Olympic Committee. Kushner, who had been approached by Infantino’s team to help structure the deal, explained that the negative response highlighted the sensitivity of football’s global stakeholders to any perceived commodification of the sport’s flagship event. He added that the experience would shape his future involvement in sports-related ventures.

The episode underscores the challenges of monetizing football’s most prestigious tournament. While FIFA remains open to exploring new revenue models, the backlash suggests that any future attempts will need to address concerns about preserving the sport’s heritage and maintaining stakeholder trust.
author: BBC Business

title: Blue Whales Track Krill in Monterey Bay with Advanced Tech
content:
Blue whales, the largest animals on Earth, remain classified as endangered despite international protections, largely because of the threat posed by collisions with commercial vessels. In the Monterey Bay region, the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) has established a Blue Whale Observatory that employs a suite of advanced monitoring technologies—acoustic sensors, satellite tagging, and high‑resolution imaging—to track whale movements and assess their interactions with shipping traffic. The observatory also studies krill, the primary food source for these whales, providing a comprehensive view of the whales’ ecological needs.

The research conducted by MBARI offers critical data for resource managers seeking to mitigate collision risks. By mapping whale migration routes and identifying high‑traffic shipping corridors, the observatory enables the development of dynamic shipping lane adjustments and speed‑limit enforcement. Simultaneously, monitoring krill populations informs habitat protection efforts, ensuring that feeding grounds remain abundant and healthy. These dual insights help create targeted conservation strategies that address both the physical safety of whales and the sustainability of their food supply.

As the Blue Whale Observatory continues to refine its monitoring techniques, the resulting evidence base strengthens policy decisions aimed at safeguarding these majestic creatures. The integration of collision risk assessments with krill ecosystem studies represents a holistic approach to whale conservation, offering a model that can be replicated in other critical marine regions worldwide.
author: Phys.org

title: Engaging Communities in Europe’s Green Neighborhoods
content:
European cities are accelerating efforts to reduce emissions, modernise building stock and overhaul energy production and consumption as the continent grapples with increasingly severe climate impacts. Municipal authorities are deploying a range of policies—from retrofitting historic structures to expanding renewable‑energy grids—in an attempt to meet EU climate targets and improve urban resilience. Despite the technical and financial resources being mobilised, officials repeatedly encounter difficulties in securing public participation and acceptance for the measures required to achieve a sustainable transformation.

Analysts and policymakers identify community engagement as the most persistent obstacle in the shift toward sustainable urban development. Studies of recent projects across several European capitals reveal that low levels of resident involvement often delay implementation, increase costs and undermine the effectiveness of climate‑focused initiatives. The consensus among experts is that strengthening dialogue with local populations, incorporating citizen feedback into planning processes and fostering transparent communication are essential steps to close the engagement gap and ensure the long‑term success of the continent’s urban climate agenda.
author: Phys.org

title: Plants' Built-In Season-Meter Predicts All Four Seasons
content:
Researchers at the University of Tsukuba have uncovered a plant “Season‑Meter” that tracks temperature changes over varying time scales to predict seasonal shifts. By monitoring two wild perennial species for two consecutive years, the team demonstrated that a trio of genes within this system records temperature data ranging from a few days to nearly five months, enabling the plants to anticipate all four seasons with remarkable accuracy. The findings, detailed in a recent PLOS One publication, highlight a sophisticated internal mechanism that mirrors, in biological terms, the way people use smartphones to plan daily outfits.

The study identified three distinct genes that each respond to temperature cues over different periods: one gene reacts within days, another over weeks, and the third over months. When their signals are integrated, the plants can forecast seasonal transitions—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—well before external cues become obvious. This multi‑scale sensing allows the plants to time flowering and other life‑history events optimally, ensuring reproductive success in fluctuating climates.

Understanding this internal timing system offers insights into plant resilience and could inform agricultural practices aimed at improving crop adaptation to climate change. By revealing how natural organisms synchronize growth with environmental rhythms, the research opens avenues for engineering crops with enhanced seasonal responsiveness.
author: Phys.org

title: AC Use Cuts U.S. Heat-Related Deaths by 50%, Saving 5,000 Lives Annually
content:
Air conditioning has become a critical safeguard against heat‑related fatalities in the United States, according to a recent study by Yale researchers. The analysis found that widespread use of air‑conditioned homes and workplaces has halved the annual number of heat‑related deaths, saving more than 5,000 lives each year. The study highlights the technology’s role as a primary adaptation tool in an era of rising temperatures and increasingly frequent heatwaves.

However, the protective effect of air conditioning is not unlimited. Researchers noted that once usage reaches a certain threshold, additional cooling does not proportionally reduce mortality risk. On days of extreme heat, the risk of heat‑related illness and death rises again even for those with access to air conditioning, underscoring that AC alone cannot fully counteract the dangers of record‑setting temperatures.

The findings suggest that while air conditioning remains an essential component of public health strategies to mitigate heat impacts, complementary measures—such as early warning systems, public cooling centers, and urban greening—are needed to protect vulnerable populations during the most severe heat events.
author: Phys.org

title: Chicago Chemists Create Single-Atom Swap Technique for Drug Discovery
content:
A team of chemists at the University of Chicago has unveiled a new technique that allows a single‑atom substitution in a molecule without altering any other part of the structure. The method, which the researchers describe as a “single‑atom edit,” uses a carefully designed catalyst to replace one atom in a target compound while leaving the surrounding framework intact. This precise manipulation could streamline the synthesis of complex organic molecules.

The approach is particularly promising for the production of pyrroles, a class of heterocyclic compounds that form the core of many pharmaceuticals, including anti‑inflammatory drugs and antiviral agents. Compared with existing routes, the new process is significantly simpler, faster, and less expensive, reducing the number of steps and the amount of hazardous reagents needed. The researchers demonstrated the technique on several pyrrole derivatives, showing that it can be applied broadly across the family of molecules.

If adopted by the pharmaceutical industry, the single‑atom edit could accelerate drug development and lower manufacturing costs. The University of Chicago team plans to further refine the catalyst and explore its application to other heterocycles, aiming to expand the toolkit available for precise molecular editing.
author: Phys.org

title: On-farm nanopore sequencing delivers rapid cattle genetic testing in Queensland
content:
Fast, on‑farm genetic testing for cattle is now practical for northern Australian producers, a University of Queensland study has shown.  In a collaboration with Meat & Livestock Australia and the Department of Primary Industries, researchers from the Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation (QAAFI) applied low‑pass nanopore sequencing on three commercial farms.  The test delivered reliable data on animal age, genomic breeding values (GBVs) and parentage for roughly 24 cattle per site, all within a 24‑hour window.

Associate Professor Elizabeth Ross highlighted that the rapid turnaround and high accuracy of the sequencing approach could transform herd management.  By generating GBVs on the farm itself, producers can make immediate breeding and culling decisions, potentially improving genetic gains and reducing costs associated with off‑site laboratory analysis.  The pilot demonstrated that the technology is robust enough for routine use in the field, even in remote northern regions.

The findings suggest that on‑farm genomic testing can become a standard tool for cattle producers seeking to accelerate genetic progress.  As the industry adopts this technology, it may lead to more efficient breeding programs and stronger, more resilient herds across Australia’s northern cattle belt.
author: Phys.org

title: Permian fossil suggests earliest flowering-plant structure discovered
content:
Angiosperms, the flowering plants that dominate today’s ecosystems, remain enigmatic in their earliest history.  While their ecological importance is unquestioned, scientists still lack a clear picture of how and when these plants first appeared.  Paleobotanists have been actively searching for clues in the fossil record, yet progress has been limited.

Researchers have examined plant remains from the late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic periods, hoping to identify the first true angiosperms.  However, the scarcity of well-preserved specimens and the difficulty of distinguishing early flowering structures from related gymnosperms have hampered definitive conclusions.  “We have an unbroken record of failure,” noted botanist Tom Harris, underscoring the persistent challenges in this field.

Despite these setbacks, new analytical techniques—such as high‑resolution imaging and molecular phylogenetics—are being applied to both fossil and extant specimens.  Continued interdisciplinary efforts are expected to refine the timeline of angiosperm evolution and to illuminate the origins of this pivotal plant group.
author: Phys.org

title: KAIST study outlines growth strategies for industrial microbial protein market
content:
KAIST researchers have released a comprehensive analysis outlining the prerequisites for establishing a viable microbial food industry, shifting the focus from feasibility to competitive leadership. Their study evaluates the sector across three critical dimensions—manufacturing processes, market dynamics, and regulatory frameworks—and identifies the specific conditions that must be met for microbial proteins to transition from laboratory prototypes to commercially scalable products.

Based on the assessment, the team proposes a set of growth strategies aimed at accelerating the development of next‑generation protein enterprises. Recommendations include optimizing fermentation technologies for cost‑effective mass production, cultivating consumer acceptance through targeted outreach, and engaging policymakers to create clear, supportive regulations. The findings are intended to guide startups, established food companies, and governmental bodies seeking to position themselves at the forefront of the emerging microbial food market.
author: Phys.org

title: Low-dose lithium studied for potential Alzheimer’s prevention
content:
Animal research has indicated that lithium orotate, a dietary supplement form of the mood‑stabilizing element, may delay the onset of dementia‑related pathology in rodent models. The findings, published in several pre‑clinical studies, showed reduced neuroinflammation and preservation of memory performance when the compound was administered at low doses. Building on this evidence, a multi‑center, double‑blind human trial is slated to begin later this year, enrolling participants with mild cognitive impairment to assess whether the same neuroprotective effects can be observed in people. The study will compare lithium orotate against a placebo over a twelve‑month period, measuring cognitive scores, brain imaging markers, and safety outcomes.

Columnist Alice Klein has examined the potential advantages and risks of lithium orotate as it moves toward clinical testing. She notes that, unlike prescription lithium carbonate, the orotate salt is marketed at lower concentrations, which could lessen the likelihood of side effects such as tremor, thyroid disruption, or renal impairment. However, Klein cautions that the supplement’s unregulated status means dosage consistency and long‑term safety remain uncertain, and that self‑medication without medical supervision could pose health hazards. The upcoming trial will provide the first rigorous data on efficacy and tolerability, determining whether lithium orotate can be considered a viable preventive strategy for dementia.
author: New Scientist

title: How the Human Body Adapts to Extreme Temperatures
content:
Scientists and health officials have issued new guidance on how individuals can better manage extreme temperatures regardless of their geographic location. The recommendations emphasize that while certain practices can improve tolerance to heat and cold, maintaining these adaptations requires consistent effort, especially during the winter months when the body’s natural acclimatization can wane.

Key strategies highlighted include gradual exposure to temperature variations, maintaining proper hydration, and wearing appropriate clothing layers to support thermoregulation. Experts note that winter can reverse some of the physiological gains achieved during warmer seasons, and that there are physiological limits to how much the body can adapt. Consequently, the guidance advises regular monitoring of body temperature and symptoms, and encourages people to seek medical advice if they experience prolonged discomfort or signs of hypothermia or heat exhaustion.

The new recommendations aim to reduce the incidence of temperature‑related health issues by promoting proactive adaptation practices. While the body’s ability to adjust has boundaries, consistent application of the outlined measures can help individuals better cope with extreme temperatures throughout the year.
author: New Scientist

title: Climate scientist uses games to aid coastal adaptation
content:
Climate scientist Sai Ravela is employing interactive game‑based simulations to assist coastal communities in developing creative adaptations to climate change. Ravela, a professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Washington, has designed a series of “serious games” that model sea‑level rise, storm surge, and erosion scenarios. The tools allow participants to experiment with a range of mitigation and adaptation measures—such as shoreline armoring, wetland restoration, and managed retreat—while seeing the projected outcomes in real time. Funded by a National Science Foundation grant and partnered with local NGOs, the games have been piloted in vulnerable regions of the Gulf Coast, the Mekong Delta, and the Netherlands.

Early trials indicate that the gaming approach fosters collaborative decision‑making and uncovers locally viable strategies that might be overlooked in traditional planning processes. Community members report increased confidence in evaluating trade‑offs between economic, environmental, and social objectives. Researchers plan to expand the platform to additional at‑risk areas and integrate the results into municipal climate‑resilience plans. By translating complex climate data into an accessible, participatory format, Ravela’s work aims to enhance preparedness and support sustainable adaptation for coastal populations worldwide.
author: MIT News

title: Study finds peptides maintain structure in Venus-like acidic conditions
content:
Scientists have reported new evidence that complex biological molecules might survive in the acidic clouds of Venus, challenging long‑standing assumptions about the planet’s hostile atmosphere. The study, published in *Nature Astronomy*, used spectroscopic data from the Venus Express orbiter and laboratory simulations to identify signatures of amino‑acid precursors in the planet’s cloud layers, which are dominated by sulfuric acid droplets and temperatures around 70 °C.

The researchers compared the spectral fingerprints of known organic compounds with the cloud‑layer measurements, finding matches that suggest a stable chemical environment capable of supporting prebiotic chemistry. While the acidic conditions would normally degrade organic matter, the team proposes that the droplets could act as protective micro‑environments, shielding molecules from ultraviolet radiation and high temperatures. This finding aligns with recent detections of phosphine and other potential biosignatures in Venusian clouds, adding a new dimension to the search for life beyond Earth.

If confirmed, the presence of complex organics in Venus’s clouds could redefine the criteria for habitable environments and inform future missions aimed at probing the planet’s upper atmosphere. The research team plans to collaborate with upcoming Venus missions to conduct in‑situ analyses and further test the stability of these molecules under Venusian conditions.
